strengths: The motivation is relevant and clearly articulated: coarse, uniform credit assignment in GRPO-style RL is a real limitation for long chain-of-thought reasoning, and using token-level entropy as a heuristic for credit assignment is a plausible and interesting idea grounded in recent literature on entropy and exploration (Cheng et al., 2025).

The paper is transparent about the relationship to DAPO, correctly distinguishing loss normalization (DAPO) from reshaping the reward itself (GTPO), and provides explicit pseudocode for both proposed algorithms.

The appendix includes a self-contained variance comparison (token-wise vs. sequence-wise averaging) via the AM-HM inequality, and the authors honestly note that entropy terms are detached from gradients to prevent reward hacking toward uniform distributions.
The limitations section acknowledges that entropy is only a heuristic and that GTPO adds computational overhead.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is fundamentally insufficient to support the central claims. The paper reports only four training-curve plots (entropy, response length, and best-of-16/32 mean reward) from a single model (Qwen2.5-32B), a single training run each, against a single baseline (DAPO). There are no held-out benchmark evaluations (e.g., AIME, MATH-500, code generation), no confidence intervals or seeds, and the claimed 'comprehensive experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks' (Section 1) are simply absent. Figures 3-4 appear to show best-of-N reward, which conflates exploration with actual capability gain.

The manuscript is an incomplete draft, not a finished paper. It contains notes-to-self and future-work placeholders in the body: 'For now, I believe we can first test the arithmetic mean and later test the geometric mean' (Section 3.4.1), 'we will set up other baselines as soon as possible' (Section 4.2), 'We will upload related resources on GitHub soon', and 'further experiments will be conducted'. The Discussion reads as working notes, including three near-identical entropy-matrix visualizations whose distinctions are never resolved experimentally.

The conclusion claims 'Ablation studies and qualitative analyses further confirm that the performance improvement is indeed due to the more refined credit assignment', but no ablation studies or qualitative analyses appear anywhere in the paper. This is an unsupported claim.

The theoretical analysis undermines rather than supports the contribution. Sections 3.5.1-3.5.2 show E[∇J_GTPO] ≈ (1+α)E[∇J_DAPO] and E[∇J_GRPO-S] ≈ (1+β)E[∇J_GRPO], i.e., the method only rescales the expected gradient magnitude without changing its direction. The authors themselves admit 'our modification primarily affects the step size of the gradient update'. This suggests the observed differences may be explainable as a learning-rate/step-size effect, and no experiment controls for this (e.g., tuning the baseline's learning rate). Additionally, the derivations rely on hand-waved approximations and a debatable i.i.d.-reward modeling assumption (treating per-token rewards as i.i.d. samples), and Eq. (18) for GRPO-S appears structurally questionable as a sequence-level surrogate.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track submission: the figures are low-resolution screenshots with UI elements and watermarks; there is inconsistent naming (GRPO-S is called 'GRPO-E' in Section 5); the reference list contains many duplicated entries (e.g., DeepSeek-R1 listed three times, DAPO twice, DPO three times) and cites blogs and YouTube videos where primary papers should be cited; and there are grammatical errors throughout ('we assigns', 'The initial phase of the experiment have validated').

The reward design has unexamined failure modes. Setting r̃_i,t = 0 for all tokens of failed sequences means incorrect sequences receive no gradient signal at all, and the d_t scaling factor, the sensitivity to α and β, and the interaction with DAPO's dynamic sampling (which filters all-fail groups) are never analyzed. With a single unexamined hyperparameter setting, the source of improvement cannot be attributed to entropy weighting versus simply injecting positive reward mass.

Reproducibility is poor: no hyperparameter values (α, β, G, ε_low, ε_high, learning rate, batch sizes), no dataset description, no training details beyond 'verl framework', and the promised code release does not exist at review time.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and timely problem: coarse-grained credit assignment in GRPO-style RL for LLM reasoning is a genuine limitation, and the motivation (high-entropy tokens marking critical decision points) is grounded in prior work (Cheng et al., 2025).

The proposed methods (GTPO token-level entropy-weighted rewards, GRPO-S sequence-level variant) are simple, clearly specified with equations and pseudocode, and the key design choice of detaching entropy terms to prevent gaming the reward is sensible.

The appendix variance analysis (AM-HM inequality argument for token-wise vs. sequence-wise averaging) is a correct, if elementary, statistical observation that provides some theoretical grounding for the loss normalization choice.
weaknesses: The paper is clearly an unfinished draft rather than a complete submission. The experiments section states 'further experiments will be conducted' and 'we will set up other baselines as soon as possible'; implementation details say 'We will upload related resources on GitHub soon'; Section 3.4 contains first-person draft notes ('For now, I believe we can first test the arithmetic mean and later test the geometric mean'). This is below the threshold of a submittable paper.

The experimental evidence does not support the central claims. There is a single model (Qwen2.5-32B), a single baseline (DAPO), no standard benchmark accuracies (e.g., AIME, MATH-500), no tables, no error bars or statistical comparisons, and only one seed apparent. The headline metrics ('mean reward over the best 32/16 responses') are non-standard training-curve statistics, and the observed differences in Figures 3-4 are small and noisy, not 'significant' as claimed.

The conclusion claims 'Ablation studies and qualitative analyses further confirm that the performance improvement is indeed due to the more refined credit assignment' — but no ablation studies or qualitative analyses appear anywhere in the paper. This is an unsupported central claim.

The theoretical analysis undercuts the paper's own contribution: Eq. (8) states E[∇J_GTPO] ≈ (1+α)E[∇J_DAPO], i.e., the modification only rescales gradient step size without changing direction. This contradicts the paper's framing that entropy weighting provides qualitatively better credit assignment, and the claim of 'convergence to a theoretically sound optimum' ignores that PPO clipping, normalization by std, and optimizer dynamics make a constant scalar rescaling non-equivalent in practice. The approximate equalities are asserted rather than proven.

The key reward identity ∑ᵢ,ₜ r̃ᵢ,ₜ = (1+α)∑ᵢ |oᵢ|rᵢ used in the theoretical analysis is asserted as 'a simple calculation' but does not obviously follow from Eq. (2), which includes the dt scaling factor and per-position entropy normalization; no derivation is given.

Serious writing and citation quality problems: duplicated references (the same works cited two to three times with variants like 'DeepSeek-AI' vs 'DeepSeek-AI, et al.', 'Rafael Rafailov and 1 others'), citations to YouTube videos and blog posts as scholarly sources, grammatical errors ('we assigns', 'achieves sequence-level... To address this'), inconsistent algorithm naming (the Discussion refers to 'GRPO-E' which is never defined), and three near-identical entropy matrices in Section 5 that differ only in highlighting with no accompanying resolution.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code released, and critical details are missing — hyperparameter values (α, β, G, clipping bounds, learning rate), the training dataset, number of training steps, and hardware. The listed limitations are acknowledged honestly but are minor compared to the missing evaluation.

The GRPO-S sequence-level importance weight (Eq. 6) is an arithmetic mean of per-token importance ratios, which is not the importance ratio of the sequence and may introduce bias; this is not analyzed, and the stated equivalence results rely on loose approximations.

strengths: The core idea—using policy entropy as a heuristic for fine-grained credit assignment in GRPO-style RL—is timely and plausibly motivated, building on recent findings (Cheng et al., 2025) that high-entropy tokens correspond to critical reasoning decision points.
The paper is clearly positioned against DAPO, and the distinction (re-shaping the reward/advantage content vs. only the loss normalization) is articulated and is a genuine conceptual difference.

Both a token-level (GTPO) and a lightweight sequence-level (GRPO-S) variant are provided, and the decision to detach entropy terms from the gradient to avoid trivially maximizing entropy is a sensible design choice that is explicitly discussed.
The appendices attempt a variance-based justification for token-level normalization, and the training-loop pseudocode makes the algorithms implementable in principle.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is far too weak to support the central claims. There is a single model (Qwen2.5-32B), a single baseline (DAPO), no GRPO comparison despite the framing, no standard benchmark results (e.g., AIME, MATH-500), no tables with numbers, no seeds or variance estimates, and no ablation study. The evidence consists of four dashboard-style screenshots of training curves; the 'best@32/best@16 reward' metrics are non-standard and no held-out test evaluation is reported.

The method does not actually solve the motivating failure case. The introduction argues that a 50-step proof with one wrong final step is unfairly penalized, but GTPO assigns r~_i,t = 0 to ALL tokens of reward-0 sequences; entropy weighting only redistributes reward within successful sequences. The paper's headline motivation (credit for correct steps in failed rollouts) is therefore unaddressed by the proposed algorithm.

The theoretical analysis does not support the claims made. The variance proof assumes i.i.d. token rewards, which the paper itself admits is violated. The convergence argument reduces to 'E[∇J_GTPO] ≈ (1+α)E[∇J_DAPO]' — but the entropy weights are token-dependent, so the modification is not a scalar multiple of the DAPO gradient; direction changes, contradicting the claim that 'only step size' is affected. The gradient identity in Eq. (18) for GRPO-S appears incorrect as written. The use of '≈' is unquantified throughout.

The manuscript reads as an unfinished internal draft. Section 3.4 contains first-person working notes ('For now, I believe we can first test the arithmetic mean and later test the geometric mean'). The Discussion contains leftover exploratory content ('Lastly, I'd like to revisit...') with three essentially identical entropy matrices distinguished only by colored highlighting, and refers to a method called 'GRPO-E' that is never defined. The conclusion claims 'Ablation studies and qualitative analyses further confirm...' but no ablations or qualitative analyses appear in the paper.

Severe reference and citation problems: duplicated and near-duplicate entries (DeepSeek-AI 2025a/b, 'DeepSeek-AI, et al.' 2025a/b/c citing the same arXiv IDs), truncated author lists ('Rafael Rafailov and 1 others'), and scholarly claims supported by blogs and YouTube videos (AI Papers Academy, WordGPT Pro, Yannic Kilcher, Hugging Face blog). A citation to Cheng et al. (2025) is inserted mid-derivation in a way that suggests the mathematical content may be borrowed rather than derived.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code is released ('will upload... soon'), hyperparameters α and β values are never specified, the training dataset is only inferable from a figure axis label ('math_dapo'), and the evaluation protocol is undefined. 'Multiple options' for the estimator definitions (arithmetic vs. geometric means) are left untested and undecided.

Multiple proposed design choices (arithmetic vs. geometric mean for H and w, three alternative entropy 'relativity' schemes) are presented as open questions rather than resolved, so the actual algorithm evaluated is ambiguous.

The 'significantly outperform' claim in the abstract is directly contradicted by the evidence provided: the shown curves overlap substantially and differences are not quantified or tested statistically.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and well-motivated problem (coarse-grained credit assignment in value-function-free RL for LLM reasoning), and the entropy-weighting idea is clearly presented with a plausible mechanistic rationale.

The proposed methods (GTPO, GRPO-S) are concretely specified with full objective functions, an algorithm box, and implementation details (group size, batch size, LR, entropy clipping thresholds, α/β values), which aids reproducibility.

Experiments cover two model scales (Qwen2.5-7B/32B), two benchmarks, multiple Pass@k metrics, a hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and training-dynamics analyses (entropy rebound, response length, clip ratio) that probe the claimed mechanism rather than reporting only end metrics.

The ablation-style appendix analysis (variance comparison of sequence-level vs token-level baselines, Appendix B.1–B.2) is a reasonable, if simple, statistical motivation for token-level normalization.
weaknesses: Limited novelty and significant overlap with prior work: the core hypothesis that high-entropy tokens mark pivotal reasoning points is taken almost verbatim from cited prior studies (Wang et al., 2025 'high-entropy minority tokens'; Cheng et al., 2025; Cui et al., 2025), and entropy-based token weighting/reward shaping for GRPO-style RL already exists. Claims of 'the first true, fine-grained, per-token credit assignment' are overstated.

Evaluation breadth is narrow and statistical support is weak: only AIME 2024/2025 are used (30 problems each), where a single problem shifts Pass@k by ~3.3%; no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, yet differences as small as +0.0115 APG (AIME 2024 mean32) are claimed as wins. No other benchmarks (e.g., MATH-500, GPQA, code) are evaluated, so generality of the claim is unsupported.

The 'theoretical guarantees' are informal and unconvincing: the argument that reward redistribution preserves the expected gradient direction rests on approximate equalities ('α1+α2 ≈ 1', 'E[Ã+] ≈ E[Â]') without quantifying the approximation error, and the GRPO-S gradient expression in Eq. (17) appears inconsistent with the policy gradient theorem. This is presented as a headline contribution but does not establish convergence as claimed.

Internal inconsistencies and clarity problems: Section 2.4.1 abruptly redefines the token-level rewards r̃ and sequence weights with geometric means, clashing with Eqs. (2)–(8); Algorithm 1 shows both GTPO and GRPO-S branches updating θ in the same iteration without clarifying whether these are separate models or combined; Appendix A.3 contains a garbled concluding sentence; Figure 2 is hard to parse.

Baseline fairness and comparison design are unclear: it is not specified whether GTPO/GRPO-S also adopt DAPO's components (Clip-Higher, Dynamic Sampling, Token-Level loss, overlong penalty) or only the plain GRPO loss, making the DAPO comparison hard to interpret. GRPO underperforming DAPO at 32B is also anomalous and unexplained.

Overclaiming of causality: the single-problem case study in Appendix E is used to assert that entropy-weighted rewards 'directly discourage' confident but incorrect decomposition; a one-example qualitative analysis cannot support such causal claims, and the DAPO failure could stem from many factors.

No limitations section, no code release statement, and the sensitivity analysis covers only three hyperparameter configurations, insufficient to characterize robustness of the α2/β2 bonus given the paper itself notes performance degrades as the entropy weight increases.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-recognized problem (coarse-grained credit assignment in outcome-reward GRPO-style training) and the core idea of repurposing policy entropy as a shaping signal at token/sequence granularity is plausible and timely.

The two-level design (token-level GTPO vs. cheaper sequence-level GRPO-S) offers a sensible precision/cost trade-off, and Algorithm 1 plus the appendix give enough implementation detail that a practitioner could attempt a reimplementation.

The empirical evaluation covers multiple configurations (AIME 2024/2025, Qwen2.5-7B/32B, Pass@k and mean32) and reports additional diagnostics (entropy trajectories, response lengths, clip ratios, hyperparameter sweeps), and the trends are internally consistent across these settings.
Appendix D.1's entropy-rebound analysis is an interesting attempt to link the shaping mechanism to a measurable training dynamic rather than only reporting final scores.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claims are not actually established. Section 2.4.2 and Appendix B.3 assert that reshaping conserves total reward and preserves the expected gradient direction, but the key identity (e.g., sum of r~+_{i,t} = (alpha1+alpha2) * sum |o_i| r_i, with alpha1+alpha2 ~ 1) does not follow from Eq. (2): the entropy-normalization term does not sum to the claimed quantity, and the used hyperparameters (alpha1=1, alpha2=0.1) do not even satisfy alpha1+alpha2 ~ 1. The entire 'theoretical guarantees' section rests on an invalid conservation argument padded with unquantified 'approx' symbols.

Appendix B.1/B.2 reduce a complicated question (variance of the policy-gradient estimator under reward shaping) to a trivial variance comparison of two means under an i.i.d. sampling assumption that does not hold for the actual estimator; this is presented as if it justifies the objective design (Conclusion 1), which it does not. Eq. (17) for the GRPO-S gradient also appears incorrect (the gradient of the averaged importance weight is not what is written).

The evaluation is far too small and noisy to support the claim of 'significant, consistent improvements' and 'a new state-of-the-art'. AIME 2024/2025 have only 30 problems each (the paper itself notes Pass@k saturates on AIME 2025 due to limited test size), yet no confidence intervals, seeds, or significance tests are reported; several reported APG differences correspond to 1-3 problems. Reporting 'maximum Pass@k' over training steps on a 30-problem test set invites selection bias.

Baseline strength is questionable: DAPO underperforms GRPO on several settings (e.g., 7B AIME 2025), and no tuning details for the baselines are given, so the gains over 'a strong DAPO baseline' may partly reflect weak baseline configuration. There is also no ablation isolating the entropy-shaping contribution from the token-level loss normalization the method already inherits from DAPO, and no comparison against closely related entropy-based credit-assignment methods that the paper itself cites (Wang et al., 2025 'high-entropy minority tokens'; Cui et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025), which makes the 'first true per-token credit assignment' novelty claim overstated.

The method specification is internally inconsistent: Section 2.2-2.3 define arithmetic-normalized rewards and importance weights, then Section 2.4.1 silently replaces them with geometric-mean formulations without stating which variant was actually evaluated; Algorithm 1 references the original equations, leaving reproducibility ambiguous. Appendix C ('Group Relative Overlong Punishment') introduces an entire additional mechanism that is never connected to any experiment, so it is unclear whether it is part of the evaluated system. There are also numerous notational errors (e.g., r~^-_{i,t} = 0 instead of r~^-_{j,t} in Eq. 3, 'Entorpy' in Figure 1).

Coverage gaps and overreach: the 7B model is missing from the AIME 2024 table, evaluation is restricted to two math benchmarks and two models from one family within only 210 training steps, and no code or artifact release is mentioned. Inverse-entropy penalties (1/H) raise unaddressed numerical stability concerns as H approaches 0. The conclusion's claim of a 'clear causal chain' from entropy weighting to performance goes beyond what the correlational evidence supports.

Presentation issues further weaken the paper: Figure 1(b) and Figure 3 are illegibly small, Figure 2 is cluttered and hard to parse, and the Discussion section (implicit curriculum learning, row/column/matrix-wise entropy comparison) proposes open design questions that arguably should have been resolved or ablated before submission.

strengths: The paper targets a real and timely problem—coarse-grained credit assignment in value-function-free RL (GRPO/DAPO) for long-chain reasoning—and the proposed entropy-weighted reward shaping is a simple, implementable idea that fits naturally into existing pipelines.

Experiments cover two model scales (Qwen2.5-7B/32B) and two benchmarks (AIME 2024/2025), with consistent improvements over GRPO and DAPO across many Pass@k settings in Table 1, plus useful auxiliary analyses: hyperparameter sensitivity (Fig. 3), entropy rebound trajectories (Fig. 5), and response-length/clip-ratio dynamics (Fig. 6) that support the claimed exploration mechanism.

The distinction from DAPO is articulated clearly (Appendix A.3): DAPO normalizes the loss over tokens but keeps the advantage constant per sequence, whereas this work reshapes the reward signal itself; the variance-reduction argument for token-level baselines (Appendix B.1) is a correct and relevant observation.
Writing is generally clear, and the two-level (token vs. sequence) design offers a sensible precision/compute trade-off for practitioners.
weaknesses: Overclaiming relative to prior work. The claim of 'the first true, fine-grained, per-token credit assignment' ignores a substantial existing literature the paper itself cites: Wang et al. (2025) on high-entropy minority tokens driving RL, Cui et al. (2025) on the entropy mechanism, Cheng et al. (2025), process reward models, PRIME-style dense rewards, etc. The core hypothesis—high-entropy tokens mark pivotal reasoning junctures—is essentially these prior findings repackaged into a reward-shaping heuristic. 'Establish a new state-of-the-art' is not substantiated beyond two AIME settings.

Theoretical analysis does not support the claimed guarantees. Section 2.4.2 rests on an approximation 'E[Ã+] ≈ E[Â]' justified by total-reward conservation with 'α1 + α2 ≈ 1', yet the experimental configuration uses α1 = 1, α2 = 0.1 (α1 + α2 = 1.1), so the stated premise does not even hold in the experiments. Moreover, preserving E[mean reward] does not imply preservation of expected advantage after per-batch mean/std normalization (Eq. 4), and gradient direction equivalence (E[∇J_GTPO] ≈ E[∇J_DAPO]) is asserted rather than proven. Equation 17 for the GRPO-S gradient appears incorrect (the derivative of the geometric/averaged importance weight does not yield the written product with an averaged log π term), and the importance-weight definition switches silently between arithmetic mean (Eq. 8) and geometric mean (§2.4.1) without reconciling the two.

Evaluation is too narrow and statistically fragile to support the central claim. AIME 2024/2025 contain only 30 problems each; differences of 0.01–0.05 in mean32 correspond to a handful of problems, yet no confidence intervals, seeds, or significance tests are reported. Pass@k is 'maximum Pass@k', which is a biased, optimistic estimator. Only one model family (Qwen2.5) and one task domain (competition math) are tested—no MATH-500, code, or out-of-distribution generalization. Notably, DAPO underperforms GRPO in several cells (e.g., AIME 2025 7B: 0.1333 vs 0.1500), raising concerns about baseline implementation strength, and no comparison against any competing fine-grained-credit or entropy-aware baseline (e.g., value-based PPO, PRIME, high-entropy token reweighting of Wang et al. 2025) is provided, so the gains cannot be attributed specifically to the entropy-weighting mechanism rather than generic hyperparameter differences.

Methodological inconsistencies and under-specified design choices. Algorithm 1 updates θ twice per iteration (once per branch), leaving unclear what single configuration produced the reported results; entropy clipping bounds (ϵ_low=0.2, ϵ_high=0.28) are introduced without any explanation of their role; the 1/Hi,t penalty in Eq. (3) diverges as entropy approaches zero with no stabilization discussed; the d_t/h_t scaling in Eqs. (2)–(3) is justified as 'adjusting for diminishing active paths' but as written the reward grows with the count of active sequences, an unexplained and possibly unintended behavior; and comparing entropies across different responses at the same timestep (column-wise in the H matrix) compares semantically unrelated tokens, which is not motivated.

The causal story is asserted more than demonstrated. The claimed chain 'entropy weighting → sustained exploration → higher Pass@k' is supported by entropy/length trajectories, but longer responses and higher clip ratios (Fig. 6) are also consistent with reward hacking of the shaping term (longer, more exploratory outputs being favored) rather than genuinely better reasoning; the single cherry-picked case study in Appendix E cannot resolve this. There is no ablation isolating the positive-bonus term from the inverse-entropy penalty term.

Reproducibility and completeness gaps: no code release is mentioned, many implementation details are absent (dynamic sampling, clip-higher settings, KL terms, how mean32 and Pass@k are computed on 30-problem sets), there is no explicit limitations section, and Appendix C describes a 'Group Relative Overlong Punishment' heuristic that is never referenced by the main-text experiments, leaving it unclear whether it was used.
